newsitem.title: UK: Gulf War Syndrome writs to be issued in Britain.
newsitem.headline: Gulf War Syndrome writs to be issued in Britain.

text.p: Lawyers for more than 1,000 British veterans who maintain they are suffering from so-called Gulf War Syndrome said on Tuesday they plan to issue writs against the defence ministry in January.
The move follows the end of a fact-finding mission by a British doctor to the United States to investigate their claims.
"The evidence coming from the United States today completely supports the conclusions that we have been drawing from the information we have been receiving," lawyer Hilary Meredith told Reuters.

"We are hoping to issue writs in January for the 1,080 veterans that we represent," she said. "The Ministry of Defence will then have to accept or deny the case and the court will give direction on a strict time scale."

The doctor, Dr Norman Jones, said there was no evidence of a single underlying cause for the illnesses that have allegedly struck thousands of veterans."It would be misleading to look for one cause for illnesses among veterans. It is much more complex than that."
He found a 30 percent rise in the number of U.S. Gulf War veterans who died from "external causes" like accidents, suicide and homicide compared with a similar group who did not serve in the Gulf.

The British government promised last month to investigate claims that British soldiers in the 1991 Gulf War were not given protective clothing when spraying pesticides suspected by some of causing the so-called syndrome.

About 51,000 Britons were involved in the war against Iraq following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait. The government has refused to recognise a specific Gulf War Syndrome and has attributed any ailments to the stress of war.
But it has been investigating some 750 veterans suffering from chronic fatigue, asthma, depression and skin complaints.
Some veterans are now confined to wheelchairs and claim their children have suffered birth defects.
